title: Is There Life on Mars? Europe's New Rover Will Dig Into Clay to Find Out!
summary:
Imagine a time billions of years ago when Mars had rivers, lakes, and maybe even an ocean. Could tiny life forms have swum in that water? Scientists think the best place to look for clues is in Martian clay—and Europe is sending a rover to dig into it!

The rover is named Rosalind Franklin, after the scientist who helped discover DNA's structure. It's part of the ExoMars mission and is set to launch in 2028. Its target? A place called Oxia Planum, a wide, low area where water once flowed. New research shows there's clay all around there, stretching 186 miles (300 kilometers) to a valley named Mawrth Vallis. That's like driving from New York City to Boston!

Why clay? Because clay minerals form in water and can trap tiny bits of ancient life, like fossils. 'We will use the instruments on board to learn about the ancient environment and if they preserve any evidence of Martian life,' said scientist Elliot Sefton-Nash. The rover has a drill to dig below the surface, where signs of life might be protected from harsh radiation.

Scientists already spotted the clay from orbit using special cameras on spacecraft. They found layers of minerals that show how water chemistry changed over time. Some think Oxia Planum might have held an ocean or experienced massive floods four billion years ago. 'We are targeting the oldest deposits, which makes the implications for early Mars very relevant,' said project scientist Jorge Vago.

So, is there life on Mars? We don't know yet. But Rosalind Franklin will be the first rover to drill deep and analyze samples right on the spot. If there are any ancient microbes hiding in that clay, we might finally find them. Get ready for a thrilling dig on the Red Planet!
why_it_matters: If we find ancient life on Mars, it would change how we think about our place in the universe and might inspire you to become a space explorer one day.

background_read: Mars once had rivers, lakes, and maybe an ocean. NASA has already sent rovers to explore, but Europe's ExoMars rover will be the first to drill deep into the soil. Rosalind Franklin (a famous scientist who helped discover DNA's structure) is a fitting name for a rover that hunts for the chemistry of life. Oxia Planum is a flat plain that scientists think was once underwater.
Article_Structure: WHO: European scientists, Elliot Sefton-Nash, and Jorge Vago
WHAT: Sending a rover named Rosalind Franklin to drill into Martian clay and search for signs of ancient life
WHERE: Oxia Planum, a wide plain on Mars
WHY: Because clay minerals form in water and can trap ancient microbes, helping us find out if life ever existed on Mars

perspectives.description: Finding life on Mars would be the greatest discovery in human history. It would prove we are not alone in the universe.
Space missions cost billions of dollars. If we don't find anything, some people say that money could have been better spent on problems here on Earth.
We might find chemical traces that suggest life, but not actual fossils. Even that would be a huge clue, but we shouldn't expect to see little aliens.
